title: Infra: GPU Fleet & Capacity + Cloud Accounts, Networking, IaC, CI/CD Playbook (Addendum)
author: Maya Thompson
body:
Summary:
This addendum consolidates operational guidance and a set of prescriptive defaults for GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD build pipelines. It is intended for on-call engineers, infra owners, and platform engineers who operate Redwood's serving runtime and deployment pipelines.

Goals:
- Reduce mean time to recovery (MTTR) for GPU capacity incidents to < 30 minutes for standard outages.
- Standardize Terraform module usage across cloud accounts to reduce drift and accelerate onboarding.
- Provide safe defaults for autoscaling, burst capacity, and network design for production Dedicated clusters.

Scope and audience:
- Applies to all GPU-backed clusters used by Hosted, Dedicated, and Private product tiers unless otherwise noted.
- Primary audience: infra owners, SRE, platform, and infra CI/CD maintainers.

Key definitions:
- capacity-manager: service that allocates GPU instances to pools and enforces quotas.
- gpu-scheduler: internal scheduling layer that assigns requests to inference nodes.
- Dedicated pool: reserved GPU capacity for a single customer or tenancy.
- Burst capacity: temporary borrowing of shared pool capacity for spikes.

Architecture overview (brief):
- Cloud accounts: each region has three accounts - control, prod-gpu, and shared-services. prod-gpu holds GPU instance pools and node autoscaling groups.
- Networking: production clusters are placed in VPCs with dedicated subnets for inference nodes and management plane; egress is NATed through shared-services. VPC peering/Transit Gateway is used for Private deployments.
- IaC: Terraform modules are the canonical source of truth for accounts, VPCs, and GPU node pools. Modules live in infra-modules repo and are consumed by per-customer and per-region stacks.
- CI/CD: Build and deploy pipelines live in the infra-ci repo; changes to modules run unit tests, a terraform plan stage, and a gated apply to a staging account before prod.

Prescriptive defaults (configs):
- Node sizes: default to p4d.24xlarge-equivalent for general-purpose inference nodes; use g5-class for cost-sensitive workloads.
- Minimum pool size: 8 GPUs for Dedicated pools (reduces fragmentation and improves scheduling).
- Autoscaling: target utilization 55% CPU/GPU, cooldown 300s, scale step 4 GPUs. Burst policy permit up to 30% of shared pool for 15 minutes with rate limiting.
- Networking: private subnets per AZ, NACL default-deny inbound, SG allow management CIDR (10.0.0.0/16) for ops, and service-to-service TLS only.

Terraform/IaC module usage (examples):
- Module: modules/gpu-node-pool
  - Inputs: region, instance_type, gpu_count, min_size, max_size, enable_burst, tags
  - Example usage snippet:
    ```hcl
    module "gpu_pool_us_east_1" {
      source        = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//gpu-node-pool"
      region        = "us-east-1"
      instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"
      gpu_count     = 8
      min_size      = 8
      max_size      = 128
      enable_burst  = true
      tags = { service = "inference", owner = "infra-team" }
    }
    ```
- Module test and gating: every module change must include a terraform validate, tflint, and terratest (Go) unit that runs in the PR pipeline. Tagging and changelog entries are required for any module with public inputs.

CI/CD and build pipeline standards:
1) Branching: main -> release branches for major infra changes. Feature branches for module changes.
2) PR checks: linters, unit tests, module contract tests, terraform plan.
3) Gated applies: staging account auto-applies on merge; production applies require a release manager approval and a successful canary (see rollout policy).
4) Rollout policy for infra changes affecting GPU pools:
   - Canary: apply new module to one non-critical region (e.g., us-west-2-dev) running a canary pool (4 GPUs).
   - Validate: run synthetic traffic workload for 30 minutes, verify scheduler latency < 200ms p50, and no unexpected allocation failures.
   - Gradual roll: 25% of regions -> 50% -> 100% with 1-hour observation windows and automated rollback on alerts.

Runbooks (high-level):
- Incident: GPU pool exhaustion (priority P0)
  1. Pager alerts SRE channel with pool ID and region.
  2. Triage: confirm metric (available_gpus < threshold) in dashboards (Dashboards/GPU Capacity).
  3. Immediate mitigations (ordered):
     a) Increase pool max_size via one-off apply to add +16 GPUs to pool (owner: infra-ops).
     b) Enable burst (if disabled) for the pool for 20m: `./scripts/ops/enable_burst.sh --pool-id <id> --duration 20m`
     c) Re-route lower-priority requests to fallback model variant using routing policy `fallback-low-cost` in capacity-manager.
  4. If scaling does not succeed in 10 minutes, open emergency cloud request to spin new instances in shared pool and notify support for customer communication.
  5. Post-incident: create postmortem, run allocation simulation locally, and schedule module change if root cause is config drift.

- Incident: Networking connectivity degraded for inference nodes
  1. Check VPC Flow Logs and route tables for recent configuration changes (use `infra-cli check-network --vpc <vpc-id>`).
  2. Validate security group changes in last 24 hours (`aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=tag:change_ticket,Values=*`).
  3. If NAT/Gateway issue, failover to alternate NAT Gateway using runbook command `infra-cli nat-failover --vpc <vpc-id>`
  4. If packet loss persists, escalate to Network Engineering and open Cloud provider support case with packet captures and traceroutes.

Operational playbook (day-to-day):
- Weekly: capacity forecast run by capacity-manager reports every Monday. Review trending and add reservations for predicted 7-day 95th percentile demand.
- Monthly: Terraform drift audit (automated) with a human review for any unchecked drift items.
- Quarterly: Chaos exercise on a non-prod region to validate autoscaling and burst behavior.

Ownership and contacts:
- infra-ops (primary): oncall@redwood.example.com
- platform-infra (owners of modules): platform@redwood.example.com
- network-eng (networking & cloud accounts): network@redwood.example.com
- capacity-team (forecasting & policies): capacity@redwood.example.com

Monitoring and SLOs (excerpts):
- GPU allocation latency: p50 < 150ms, p95 < 500ms (SLO target 99.9%).
- Pool availability: 99.95% monthly uptime for Dedicated pools.
- Autoscale success rate: 99% of scale events complete within 4 minutes.

Common CLI commands and snippets:
- Check pool status:
  `infra-cli pool status --pool-id pool-prod-us-east-1`
- Trigger scale-up (ops only):
  `infra-cli pool scale --pool-id pool-prod-us-east-1 --delta 16 --reason "incident mitigation"`
- Run terraform plan for region stack:
  `cd infra-stacks/us-east-1 && terragrunt plan --terragrunt-non-interactive`

Security and compliance notes:
- KMS keys: all GPU node pools encrypt local caches with customer keys where required; module input `kms_key_id` must be supplied for restricted customers.
- Audit logging: all scaling and burst events are logged to audit-log S3 with 90-day retention by default; extended retention is an add-on.

Appendix: troubleshooting checklist (short)
- If instance provisioning fails: check cloud quota and account limits, then check instance type availability in AZs.
- If scheduler shows high queue length: verify prefix cache hit-rate and KV cache size; restart gpu-scheduler if memory leak suspected.
- If terraform apply fails in prod: revert to last known-good module tag and run a targeted apply to the minimally impacted stack.

Related docs and templates:
- infra runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
- Terraform module guide: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026
- CI/CD gating policy: /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/terraform-pipeline-standards-2025 (link internal)
